To stint means to limit or restrict the supply of something — usually to a degree that feels too small, too tight, or not enough. When you stint on something, you are deliberately holding back, giving less than what is really needed, deserved, or expected.

The word carries a sense of excessive stinginess or tightfistedness — not just being careful, but being so sparing that it becomes noticeable, even unfair.

Imagine you are cooking pasta for your family. You have a full bag of sauce, but you squeeze out only a tiny drop onto each plate, even though everyone is hungry. You are stinting on the sauce. You are holding back. You are giving far less than what the situation calls for.

Now imagine a company that could easily pay its workers fair wages, but instead keeps cutting their pay and benefits. The company is stinting its workers. It is giving them less than what they deserve.

That uncomfortable gap — between what could or should be given and what actually is given — is exactly where the word "stint" lives.

The verb "stint" shows up in a few reliable patterns. Getting familiar with each one will make the word feel completely natural to you.

1. "Stint on something"
This is the most common pattern. It means to be overly sparing in the use or provision of something.

  • "Don't stint on the butter when making this cake — it needs a full cup."
  • "The hotel clearly stinted on cleaning. The rooms were dusty and the towels were thin."
  • "He stinted on sleep for weeks to meet his deadline."

2. "Not stint on something"
Used in the negative, this means to be generous — to give freely without holding back. This is very common because people often use the negative to express praise or encouragement.

  • "She never stints on kindness — she gives her time and energy to everyone who needs it."
  • "The chef did not stint on quality ingredients, and it showed in every bite."

3. "Stint someone of something" (slightly more formal or older usage)
This means to deprive someone of their fair or full share of something.

  • "The landlord stinted the tenants of basic repairs and hot water for months."
  • "She felt she had been stinted of a proper childhood."

4. "Stint yourself"
To deprive yourself of something you need or deserve, usually for the sake of someone else.

  • "She stinted herself so her children could have everything they needed."
  • "Don't stint yourself — there is plenty of food for everyone."

"Stint" is not a neutral word. It carries a slight negative charge. It suggests that the restriction is unwarranted — that there was room to be more generous, but someone chose not to be. It's the word you use when the tightening of supply feels mean, unhealthy, or unjust in some way.

This is why the phrase "don't stint" is so encouraging — it is essentially saying: "You have enough. Be generous. Don't hold back unnecessarily."

It is different from, say, the word "save," which sounds wise and deliberate. Stinting sounds like squeezing, pinching, cutting corners. It leaves people or things with less than they should have.
Quick Contrast to Sharpen Your Understanding

SituationThe right word
You carefully save money for retirementSaving / being thrifty
You give your guests barely any food even though you have plentyStinting on food
You pour a rich, generous amount of cream into a dishNot stinting on the cream
A company denies workers fair pay despite huge profitsStinting its workers

Whenever you see or hear "stint" used as a verb, ask yourself: "Is someone giving, using, or allowing less than what is really needed or deserved?" If the answer is yes, the word is being used correctly.

That's it — that single question captures everything the verb "stint" means.
